RDS: AWS patches the OS and database engine; you manage data, users and access. Lambda: AWS manages servers, OS and runtime; you manage code and permissions. Customers always own their data and IAM.

cards.eli12: Access keys let software/CLI authenticate to AWS; protect them like passwords.
cards.definition: Long-term credentials made of an access key ID and a secret access key, used for programmatic access to AWS through the CLI, SDKs or API. Never share them or embed them in code; rotate them regularly and prefer IAM roles (temporary credentials) where possible.
cards.official: Access key: A pair of an access key ID and a secret access key, used to sign API requests to AWS.

cards.eli12: Account rules can require stronger IAM user passwords.
cards.definition: IAM account password policy defines password requirements for IAM users.
cards.official: You can set a custom password policy on your AWS account to specify complexity requirements and mandatory rotation periods ...

cards.eli12: An IAM user is an identity with credentials and permissions.
cards.definition: IAM identity representing a person or workload with long-term credentials when used.
cards.official: IAM users aren't separate accounts; they're individual users within your account. Each user has their own password for access to the AWS Management Console.

cards.eli12: Put users in a group so they can share permissions.
cards.definition: Collection of IAM users used to assign permissions to multiple users.
cards.official: A collection of IAM users. You can use IAM groups to simplify specifying and managing permissions for multiple users.

cards.term: IAM Managed Policies vs Customer Managed Policies
cards.eli12: Policies can be AWS-managed or customer-managed and attached to identities.
cards.definition: Managed policies are reusable IAM policies maintained by AWS or by the customer.

cards.eli12: You can write permissions tailored to a specific need.
cards.definition: Customer-defined IAM policies specify allowed or denied actions and resources.
cards.official: Inline policy: An IAM policy that's embedded in a single IAM user, group, or role.

cards.hint: ROLE = borrow access to another account
cards.eli12: A role can grant temporary access across AWS accounts without sharing passwords.
cards.definition: IAM roles can enable secure cross-account access using temporary credentials.
cards.official: IAM roles are an IAM identity that you can create in your account that has specific permissions that determine what the identity can and can't do. However, instead of being uniquely associated with one person, a role is intended to be assumable by anyone who needs it.

cards.eli12: Users can access AWS using identities from another trusted identity provider.
cards.definition: Federation lets external identities authenticate and receive AWS access without separate long-term IAM user credentials.
cards.official: With identity federation in AWS, external identities (federated users) are granted secure access to resources in an AWS account without having to create IAM users. These external identities can come from a corporate identity store (such as LDAP or Windows Active Directory) or from a third party (such as Login with Amazon, Facebook, or Google).

cards.eli12: Searchable AWS troubleshooting and technical knowledge articles.
cards.definition: AWS technical knowledge resource for common questions and issues.

cards.eli12: Official AWS articles about security practices and updates.
cards.definition: Official AWS security guidance and information resource.

cards.eli12: Where eligible customers create and manage AWS Support cases.
cards.definition: AWS portal for support cases and support-related resources.

cards.eli12: AWS technical experts who help customers understand and design AWS solutions.
cards.definition: AWS technical professionals who provide architectural guidance to customers.

cards.eli12: Apps can retrieve AWS Health events through an API.
cards.definition: Programmatic access to the same AWS Health event information shown in the Health Dashboard, for automating responses. Requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise Support plan.

cards.eli12: AWS team/resource for reporting abuse involving AWS resources.
cards.definition: The AWS team that handles reports of abuse involving AWS resources — spam, port scanning, DDoS attacks, phishing or malware hosted on AWS. Report suspected abuse to them (abuse report form).

cards.eli12: Resources and workloads operate in a cloud environment.
cards.definition: Deployment model in which workloads run in cloud infrastructure.
cards.official: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, database, storage, applications, and other IT resources through a cloud services platform via the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

cards.eli12: Some systems stay on-prem while others run in AWS and connect together.
cards.definition: Deployment model combining on-premises infrastructure with cloud resources.

cards.eli12: Organization owns/operates infrastructure in its own facilities or colocations.
cards.definition: Traditional deployment model using customer-controlled data-center infrastructure.

cards.eli12: Manual actions can work once; repeated environments benefit from IaC/automation.
cards.definition: Choose provisioning methods based on whether operations are ad hoc or need consistent repeatability.

cards.eli12: Use more than one Region for needs such as disaster recovery, business continuity, low latency, or data sovereignty.
cards.definition: Using workloads/resources across multiple AWS Regions to meet geographic, resilience, or regulatory requirements.
cards.official: Go global in minutes: Easily deploy your application in multiple regions around the world with just a few clicks. This means you can provide lower latency and a better experience for your customers at minimal cost.

cards.term: Availability Zones and Single Points of Failure
cards.eli12: Separate AZs are designed so one failure does not become a shared single point of failure.
cards.definition: Running a workload in only one AZ creates a single point of failure. Deploying across two or more AZs (e.g., EC2 behind a load balancer, RDS Multi-AZ) keeps the application available if one AZ fails.
cards.official: A distinct location within a Region that's insulated from failures in other Availability Zones, and provides inexpensive, low-latency network connectivity to other Availability Zones in the same Region.

cards.eli12: Balanced CPU, memory, and networking for common workloads.
cards.definition: Balanced compute, memory and networking. Use for web servers, code repositories, small/medium databases and dev/test environments.
cards.official: General purpose – Provide a balance of compute, memory, and networking resources. These instances are ideal for applications that use these resources in equal proportions, such as web servers and code repositories.

cards.eli12: Best when the workload needs lots of processor power.
cards.definition: High-performance processors for compute-bound workloads: batch processing, media transcoding, high-performance web servers, scientific modeling, dedicated gaming servers and ML inference.
cards.official: Compute optimized – Designed for compute intensive applications that benefit from high performance processors. These instances are ideal for batch processing workloads, media transcoding, high performance web servers, high performance computing (HPC), scientific modeling, dedicated gaming servers, ad server engines, and machine learning inference.

cards.eli12: Best when applications need lots of RAM.
cards.definition: Large amounts of RAM for workloads that process big data sets in memory: in-memory databases and caches, real-time big data analytics.
cards.official: Memory optimized – Designed to deliver fast performance for workloads that process large data sets in memory.

cards.eli12: Best for workloads needing high local storage throughput/IO.
cards.definition: High, sequential read/write access to very large data sets on local storage (high IOPS): data warehousing, distributed file systems, high-frequency OLTP databases.
cards.official: Storage optimized – Designed for workloads that require high, sequential read and write access to very large data sets on local storage. They are optimized to deliver tens of thousands of low-latency, random I/O operations per second (IOPS) to applications.

cards.eli12: Uses hardware accelerators for workloads such as graphics or specialized computation.
cards.definition: Use hardware accelerators (GPUs, FPGAs, AWS Trainium/Inferentia) for floating-point calculations, graphics processing, video encoding and machine learning training/inference.
cards.official: Accelerated computing – Use hardware accelerators, or co-processors, to perform functions, such as floating point number calculations, graphics processing, or data pattern matching, more efficiently than is possible in software running on CPUs.

cards.eli12: On EC2 you manage more database/infrastructure work; RDS/Aurora manage more for you.
cards.definition: Running a database on EC2 gives full control (any engine/version, OS access) but you handle OS and database patching, backups, scaling and high availability. A managed service such as Amazon RDS or DynamoDB shifts those tasks to AWS so you focus on data and schema.

cards.eli12: Default S3 class for frequently accessed data needing high availability.
cards.definition: Default S3 storage class for frequently accessed data. Millisecond access, data stored across at least 3 AZs, no retrieval fees and no minimum storage duration — but the highest storage price of the S3 classes.
cards.official: The default storage class. If you don't specify the storage class when you upload an object, Amazon S3 assigns the S3 Standard storage class.

cards.hint: IA = INFREQUENT but fast when needed
cards.eli12: Lower storage cost for data accessed less often, with retrieval charges.
cards.definition: S3 Infrequent Access: for long-lived data accessed less than once a month that still needs millisecond access when requested. Stored across at least 3 AZs. Cheaper storage than Standard, but charges a per-GB retrieval fee and has a 30-day minimum storage duration.
cards.official: Amazon S3 stores the object data redundantly across multiple geographically separated Availability Zones (similar to the S3 Standard storage class).

cards.hint: ONE ZONE = cheaper, not multi-AZ resilient
cards.eli12: Infrequently accessed data stored in one AZ; use for recreatable data.
cards.definition: Like Standard-IA but stores data in a single Availability Zone, so it costs about 20% less — and the data is lost if that AZ is destroyed. Per-GB retrieval fee and 30-day minimum. Use for infrequently accessed data you can re-create (e.g., secondary backup copies).
cards.official: Amazon S3 stores the object data in only one Availability Zone, which makes it less expensive than S3 Standard-IA. However, the data is not resilient to the physical loss of the Availability Zone resulting from disasters, such as earthquakes and floods.

cards.eli12: Automatically optimizes storage cost when access patterns change or are unknown.
cards.definition: S3 storage class that automatically moves objects between cost-effective access tiers based on changing access patterns, without performance impact or retrieval fees. Charges a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object instead. Best when access patterns are unknown or change.
cards.official: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is an Amazon S3 storage class that's designed to optimize storage costs by automatically moving data to the most cost-effective access tier, without performance impact or operational overhead.

cards.eli12: Archive pricing for rarely accessed data that still needs millisecond retrieval.
cards.definition: Archive storage class for rarely accessed data (about once a quarter) that still needs millisecond retrieval. Lower storage cost than Standard-IA, higher retrieval cost; 90-day minimum storage duration.
cards.official: Use for long-term data that's rarely accessed and requires milliseconds retrieval. Data in this storage class is available for real-time access.

cards.eli12: Low-cost archive when retrieval can take minutes to hours.
cards.definition: Low-cost archive storage for data accessed 1–2 times a year that doesn't need immediate access. Retrieval options: Expedited (1–5 minutes), Standard (3–5 hours), Bulk (5–12 hours, free). 90-day minimum storage duration.
cards.official: Use for archives where portions of the data might need to be retrieved in minutes. Data in this storage class is archived, and not available for real-time access.

cards.eli12: Very low-cost long-term archive when retrieval can wait hours.
cards.definition: Lowest-cost S3 storage class, for long-term retention (7–10+ years, e.g., compliance) of data accessed once or twice a year. Retrieval within 12 hours (Standard) or 48 hours (Bulk). 180-day minimum storage duration. Replaces magnetic tape.
cards.official: Use for archiving data that rarely needs to be accessed. Data in this storage class is archived, and not available for real-time access.

cards.eli12: Rules automatically move objects to cheaper classes or expire them.
cards.definition: Rules that automatically transition objects to cheaper storage classes after a set time (e.g., Standard → Standard-IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90 days) and expire (delete) objects. Use when access patterns are predictable; use Intelligent-Tiering when they aren't.

cards.eli12: Very fast temporary block storage; data can disappear when the instance stops/terminates depending on lifecycle.
cards.definition: Temporary block storage on disks physically attached to the EC2 host. Very high I/O and included in the instance price, but data is lost when the instance is stopped, hibernated or terminated. Use only for buffers, caches and scratch data.

cards.term: Object vs Block vs File Storage
cards.eli12: Choose storage by how applications need to access data.
cards.definition: Object = whole files with metadata in a flat namespace, accessed by API (Amazon S3). Block = raw volumes attached to one instance, best for OS/databases (Amazon EBS, instance store). File = shared hierarchical file system many servers mount (Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx).

cards.eli12: Reserved Instance discounts and flexibility depend on offering, scope, platform, family/size, and other attributes.
cards.definition: Regional RIs apply the discount to usage in any AZ in the Region and (for Linux) to any size within the same instance family, but do not reserve capacity. Zonal RIs reserve capacity in one AZ but have no size flexibility. Convertible RIs can be exchanged for different instance families, OS or tenancy.

cards.hint: RI benefits can SHARE across accounts
cards.eli12: With consolidated billing, qualifying RI pricing benefits can apply across accounts in an organization under AWS rules.
cards.definition: With consolidated billing, Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts purchased in one account can apply to matching usage in other accounts in the organization. The management account can turn this sharing off.
cards.official: Consolidated billing: A feature of the AWS Organizations service for consolidating payment for multiple AWS accounts. You create an organization that contains your AWS accounts, and you use the management account of your organization to pay for all member accounts.

cards.hint: IN often cheaper/free; OUT often costs
cards.eli12: Know that network data transfer charges vary by direction and location.
cards.definition: Data transferred into AWS from the internet is free. Data transferred out to the internet is charged per GB. Transfer between Regions is charged, and transfer between AZs is generally charged; transfer within the same AZ over private IPs is free. Using CloudFront can lower data-transfer-out costs.

cards.eli12: Storage price varies by class, access frequency, retrieval, performance, and durability/availability characteristics.
cards.definition: Storage pricing depends on the service and class. S3 charges per GB-month stored, plus requests, retrieval fees (IA and Glacier classes) and data transferred out; colder classes cost less to store but more to retrieve. EBS charges for provisioned GB whether used or not; EFS charges for GB actually used.

cards.eli12: AWS publishes technical documentation, whitepapers, blogs, and guides.
cards.definition: Official AWS websites provide technical and best-practice resources for customers.

cards.term: AWS Partners: ISVs vs System Integrators
cards.eli12: Partners may sell software or help customers implement and integrate solutions.
cards.definition: AWS Partner Network includes independent software vendors and system integrators with different roles.

cards.eli12: AWS Partners can receive enablement and business benefits.
cards.definition: Partner benefits can include training/certification, events, and volume-related benefits.

cards.eli12: Marketplace is more than a store: it can support procurement, cost management, governance, and entitlements.
cards.definition: AWS Marketplace helps customers discover, procure, govern, and manage third-party software and services.
cards.official: AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalog that customers can use to find, buy, deploy, and manage third-party software, data, and services to build solutions and run their businesses. AWS Marketplace includes thousands of software listings from popular categories such as security, business applications, machine learning, and data products across specific industries, such as healthcare, financial services, and telecommunications.

cards.eli12: The website where you click around to use AWS.
cards.definition: Web-based interface for accessing and managing AWS services. For Regional services, the console is scoped to the Region you select.
cards.official: The AWS Management Console is a web-based application that contains and provides centralized access to all individual AWS service consoles.
cards.notes: In scope for CLF-C02. Console = clicking; CLI/SDK = programmatic.

cards.eli12: A command line inside the AWS console, with nothing to install.
cards.definition: Browser-based shell launched from the AWS Management Console, already signed in with your console credentials and preinstalled with the AWS CLI. No extra charge.
cards.official: AWS CloudShell is a browser-based shell that makes it easier to securely manage, explore, and interact with your AWS ...

cards.hint: IaC in a REAL programming language
cards.eli12: Describe your infrastructure with code like Python or TypeScript instead of a template file.
cards.definition: Open-source framework for defining cloud infrastructure in familiar programming languages (TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Go). It deploys through AWS CloudFormation.
cards.official: AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) is an open-source software development framework for defining your cloud infrastructure in code and provisioning it through CloudFormation.
cards.notes: Think IaC → CloudFormation (templates) or CDK (code).

cards.hint: ARN = unique ADDRESS of a resource
cards.eli12: Every AWS thing has its own unique ID string.
cards.definition: Unique identifier for an AWS resource, used to refer to it unambiguously across AWS, for example in IAM policies. Format: arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource.
cards.notes: Usually shown under a resource's properties.

cards.hint: Give me a COMPUTER, I'll do the rest
cards.eli12: Rent the kitchen, make your own pizza.
cards.definition: Cloud model that provides the basic building blocks: networking, virtual or dedicated computers, and storage. The customer manages the OS, apps and data. AWS example: Amazon EC2.
cards.notes: Exam: 'rent virtual servers and install own OS' → IaaS (EC2).

cards.hint: Give me somewhere to RUN MY CODE
cards.eli12: Pick your pizza; someone else runs the kitchen.
cards.definition: Cloud model where the provider manages the underlying infrastructure (hardware, OS, runtime) so you focus on deploying and managing your applications. AWS example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
cards.notes: Exam: 'upload code without managing servers' → PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk).

cards.eli12: Order a pizza that's already made.
cards.definition: Complete product that the provider runs and manages; you just use it (e.g., web-based email, Microsoft 365, Salesforce). You manage only your data and settings.
cards.notes: Exam: 'use online email without maintaining servers' → SaaS.

cards.hint: stay UP: run in MULTIPLE AZs
cards.eli12: If one data center fails, the app keeps running.
cards.definition: Ability of a system to stay operational with minimal downtime by removing single points of failure, for example running in multiple Availability Zones behind Elastic Load Balancing.
cards.notes: S3 is highly available by default; a single EC2 instance is not (deploy 2+ AZs).

cards.hint: keeps working even when PARTS FAIL
cards.eli12: Like a spare tire: something breaks and you keep driving.
cards.definition: Ability of a system to keep operating without interruption when one or more components fail, using redundancy and automatic failover (e.g., RDS Multi-AZ standby).

cards.eli12: Your files won't disappear.
cards.definition: How likely stored data is to stay intact and not be lost over time. Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability by storing data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones.
cards.notes: Durability = data not lost. Availability = data reachable right now.

cards.hint: Backup → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Multi-site (more cost = faster recovery)
cards.eli12: Four ways to be ready for a disaster, from cheap and slow to expensive and instant.
cards.definition: AWS DR strategies from lowest cost and slowest recovery to highest cost and fastest: Backup and restore; Pilot light (data replicated, core infrastructure ready but idle); Warm standby (scaled-down but fully working copy running); Multi-site active/active (full production in multiple Regions).
cards.official: With the pilot light approach, you replicate your data from one Region to another and provision a copy of your core workload infrastructure. The warm standby approach involves ensuring that there is a scaled down, but fully functional, copy of your production environment in another Region.
cards.notes: Lower RTO/RPO = more expensive strategy.

cards.hint: RTO = TIME to get back UP
cards.eli12: How long you can afford to be down.
cards.definition: Maximum acceptable delay between a service interruption and the restoration of service.
cards.notes: Time → RTO. Data loss → RPO.

cards.hint: RPO = how much DATA you can lose (Point in time)
cards.eli12: How far back in time you can afford to lose data.
cards.definition: Maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point, which defines how much data loss is acceptable.

cards.eli12: A special AWS Region for US government and regulated data.
cards.definition: Isolated AWS Regions for sensitive US government workloads and regulated industries, built to meet requirements such as ITAR, FedRAMP and DoD SRG.
cards.official: AWS GovCloud (US) is an isolated AWS Region that hosts sensitive workloads in the cloud, ensuring that this work meets the US government's regulatory and compliance requirements.

cards.eli12: A public IP address that doesn't change when you restart.
cards.definition: Static public IPv4 address allocated to your account. You can attach it to an instance and quickly remap it to another instance to mask a failure. Public IPv4 addresses are billed.
cards.official: A fixed (static) IP address that you have allocated in Amazon EC2 or Amazon VPC and then attached to an instance. Elastic IP addresses are associated with your account, not a specific instance.

cards.eli12: Like reselling a gym membership you no longer use.
cards.definition: Marketplace where you can sell unused Standard Reserved Instances to other AWS customers, or buy RIs with shorter remaining terms. Convertible RIs can't be sold there.
cards.notes: Standard RI = bigger discount, can be sold. Convertible RI = can be exchanged, can't be sold.

cards.eli12: Nobody gets automatic trust, even inside the network.
cards.definition: Security model that grants no trust based on network location. Every request is authenticated and authorized based on identity, so identity becomes the main security perimeter. On AWS: IAM, MFA, least privilege, IAM Identity Center.

cards.eli12: A permission slip written in JSON.
cards.definition: JSON document that defines permissions. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (API operations), Resource (ARNs) and an optional Condition. Attach policies to users, groups or roles. An explicit Deny always wins.

cards.eli12: Labels on your resources so you can find, organize and bill them.
cards.definition: Tags are key-value labels on AWS resources used to organize, search, control access and track costs. AWS Resource Groups collect resources that share tags so you can view and manage them together.
cards.official: A tag is a label that you or AWS assigns to an AWS resource. Each tag consists of a key and a value.
cards.notes: Handy for per-project IAM policies and cost tracking.

cards.hint: count ALL the costs, not just servers
cards.eli12: Add up everything (hardware, power, people) to compare on-premises with cloud.
cards.definition: Estimate of all direct and indirect costs of running a solution (hardware, software, facilities, power, cooling, staff), used to compare on-premises with the cloud. Migration Evaluator builds a TCO-based business case.

cards.hint: bring your VM IMAGES in or out
cards.eli12: Copy your existing virtual machines into AWS.
cards.definition: Imports virtual machine images from your existing environment (e.g., VMware, Microsoft Hyper-V) as Amazon EC2 instances, and exports them back.

cards.eli12: Use some AWS services for free while you learn.
cards.definition: Lets customers try AWS services at no charge up to set limits, including always-free usage on some services (e.g., AWS Lambda) and free credits or trial periods for new accounts.
cards.notes: Set a budget alert so you don't go past the free limits.

cards.eli12: AWS promises a level of uptime; if they miss it you get credits back.
cards.definition: AWS's commitment to a monthly uptime percentage for a service (e.g., Amazon EC2's Region-level SLA is 99.99%). If AWS misses it, customers can claim service credits.

cards.hint: PEN TEST approved services: no permission needed
cards.eli12: You can run security tests on your own stuff on certain services without asking first.
cards.definition: Customers can run penetration tests on their own resources for a list of approved services (e.g., EC2, RDS, Lambda, CloudFront) without prior approval. DoS/DDoS simulations and attacks on AWS infrastructure are not allowed without separate approval.

cards.eli12: Many locks: a fence, a door and a safe.
cards.definition: Security approach that applies multiple layers of controls (edge and WAF, network and security groups, compute, application, data encryption, IAM) so that if one layer fails, others still protect.

cards.eli12: Keep secrets secret, data unchanged, and systems up.
cards.definition: Core security model. Confidentiality: only authorized access (encryption, IAM). Integrity: data is accurate and unaltered (hashing, checksums). Availability: systems and data are reachable when needed (Multi-AZ, backups).

cards.hint: NO SERVERS to manage; pay per use
cards.eli12: You give AWS code and it runs it.
cards.definition: Model where AWS manages the servers: you don't provision or patch infrastructure, it scales automatically and you pay for what you use (e.g., AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, DynamoDB, S3). Cold starts can add latency.

cards.eli12: Get it yourself, from anywhere, shared, grows on demand, pay for what you use.
cards.definition: On-demand self-service; broad network access; multi-tenancy and resource pooling; rapid elasticity and scalability; measured service (you pay for what you use).

cards.eli12: What you're not allowed to do with AWS.
cards.definition: Policy that prohibits using AWS for illegal, harmful or offensive activities, security violations (e.g., unauthorized access), network abuse and email or message abuse (spam). Report violations to AWS Trust & Safety.

cards.eli12: A hat you put on to get permissions for a while.
cards.definition: IAM identity with permissions that can be assumed by AWS services (e.g., an EC2 instance role), users or other accounts. It gives temporary credentials instead of a long-term password or access keys.
cards.notes: Give AWS services permissions with roles, never with access keys.

cards.eli12: Gives out short-lived passes instead of permanent keys.
cards.definition: Issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials that expire after a set time. Used when assuming IAM roles, for identity federation and for cross-account access.

cards.hint: REPORT = all users' credentials; ADVISOR = what each user actually uses
cards.eli12: Two tools that show who has what and what they really use.
cards.definition: IAM security tools. The credentials report (account level) lists all users and the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA. Access Advisor/last accessed (user level) shows which services a user can reach and when they last used them, so you can remove unused permissions.
cards.notes: Helps enforce least privilege.

cards.hint: who OUTSIDE can reach my resources?
cards.eli12: Finds anything you've accidentally shared with outsiders.
cards.definition: Identifies resources (e.g., S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, Lambda functions, Secrets Manager secrets) that are shared with an external entity, based on a zone of trust you define (your account or organization).

cards.eli12: A ceiling on what accounts in your organization can ever do.
cards.definition: AWS Organizations policies attached to the organization root, OUs or accounts that set the maximum permissions available. SCPs don't grant permissions themselves, and they don't restrict the management account.

cards.eli12: The door numbers for common ways to connect to a server.
cards.definition: Ports to know: 22 = SSH (Linux login, also SFTP); 21 = FTP; 80 = HTTP; 443 = HTTPS; 3389 = RDP (Windows remote desktop). Security groups allow or block these.

cards.hint: script that runs at FIRST BOOT
cards.eli12: Instructions an instance follows the first time it starts.
cards.definition: Script you provide at launch that runs once, as root, when the instance first boots. Used to automate setup such as installing updates and software.

cards.eli12: Log in to a server straight from the AWS console.
cards.definition: Connects to an EC2 instance over SSH from the browser in the AWS console, using a temporary key, with no key file to manage. (Systems Manager Session Manager is another way that doesn't need port 22.)

cards.eli12: A saved copy of a server setup you can launch again and again.
cards.definition: Template containing the OS, software and configuration used to launch EC2 instances. Use public AWS AMIs, your own custom AMIs (faster boot because software is pre-installed) or AWS Marketplace AMIs. AMIs are Region-specific but can be copied.

cards.eli12: A photo of your hard drive at one moment.
cards.definition: Point-in-time, incremental backups of EBS volumes stored in S3. You can copy them across AZs or Regions to move volumes. Features: Snapshot Archive (cheaper tier, slower restore) and Recycle Bin (recover accidentally deleted snapshots).
cards.notes: An EBS volume is tied to one AZ; use a snapshot to move it.

cards.hint: EFS for files you RARELY open
cards.eli12: Cheaper shelf in the shared file system for files you don't use often.
cards.definition: Lower-cost EFS storage class for files not accessed every day. A lifecycle policy automatically moves files there based on when they were last accessed.

cards.hint: ALB = HTTP (L7) · NLB = TCP/UDP fast (L4) · GWLB = firewalls (L3)
cards.eli12: Three kinds of traffic cops for different kinds of traffic.
cards.definition: Application Load Balancer: HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC at Layer 7, routes by URL path or host. Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP at Layer 4, ultra-high performance, static IP. Gateway Load Balancer: Layer 3, routes traffic through third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls.

cards.eli12: Rules for when to add or remove servers.
cards.definition: Ways an Auto Scaling group scales: manual; dynamic (simple/step scaling or target tracking, e.g., keep CPU at 40%); scheduled (known times); predictive (machine learning forecasts the load ahead of time).

cards.eli12: A twin database in another data center ready to take over.
cards.definition: Keeps a synchronous standby copy of the RDS database in another AZ and fails over to it automatically if the primary fails. Used for high availability, not to scale reads.
cards.notes: Read Replica = performance. Multi-AZ = availability.

cards.hint: DAX = cache in front of DynamoDB
cards.eli12: Super-fast memory layer for DynamoDB.
cards.definition: Fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that gives microsecond read latency for frequently read items.
cards.notes: DAX is only for DynamoDB; ElastiCache works with other databases.

cards.term: S3 Bucket Policies & Block Public Access
cards.hint: BUCKET POLICY = JSON rules on the bucket
cards.eli12: Rules on a bucket saying who can get in.
cards.definition: Bucket policies are JSON resource-based policies that control access to a bucket (e.g., make a website public, allow another account, require encryption). Block Public Access settings (on by default) stop data from being made public by mistake.

cards.eli12: Undo button for your files.
cards.definition: Bucket setting that keeps multiple versions of each object. Protects against accidental deletes (a delete adds a delete marker) and lets you roll back to a previous version.

cards.hint: CRR = other Region · SRR = same Region
cards.eli12: Automatic copies of your files into another bucket.
cards.definition: Asynchronously copies objects to another bucket. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is for compliance and lower-latency access in another Region; Same-Region Replication (SRR) is for log aggregation or copying between accounts. Versioning must be on.

cards.eli12: Super-fast S3 storage kept in a single data center area.
cards.definition: High-performance S3 storage class that stores data in a single AZ (in directory buckets) for single-digit millisecond access. Used for data-intensive apps like ML training and analytics.

cards.eli12: S3 locks your files; you can lock them yourself first, too.
cards.definition: Server-side encryption: S3 encrypts objects when it stores them (on by default for new objects). Client-side encryption: you encrypt the data before uploading it.

cards.eli12: Uses AWS's fast network to speed up long-distance uploads.
cards.definition: Speeds up long-distance uploads and downloads to S3 by routing them through the nearest edge location, then over the AWS global network.

cards.eli12: A lunchbox with the app and everything it needs, so it runs the same anywhere.
cards.definition: Docker packages an app and its dependencies into a container image that runs the same on any OS. Containers are lighter than VMs because they share the host's kernel. On AWS, images are stored in ECR and run on ECS, EKS or Fargate.

cards.eli12: Collects every app's diary in one place.
cards.definition: Collects and stores logs from apps, EC2 (via the CloudWatch agent), Lambda, VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail and more, for real-time monitoring and search. Retention is adjustable.

cards.hint: ALARM when estimated CHARGES go up
cards.eli12: Alerts you when your AWS bill passes a number.
cards.definition: CloudWatch alarm on the EstimatedCharges billing metric. Billing data is stored in us-east-1 and covers your whole account's estimated charges. AWS Budgets offers more options.

cards.eli12: Watches your spending and flags anything weird.
cards.definition: Uses machine learning to monitor cost and usage, detect unusual spend, show root-cause analysis and send alerts (individual or summary) by email or SNS.

cards.hint: log of IP TRAFFIC in your VPC
cards.eli12: A record of what network traffic came and went.
cards.definition: Captures information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in a VPC, subnet or ENI. Sent to CloudWatch Logs or S3 to troubleshoot connectivity and security.

cards.eli12: A private bridge between two networks.
cards.definition: Privately connects two VPCs over the AWS network so they act as if they're in the same network. IP ranges must not overlap, and peering isn't transitive (A↔B and B↔C doesn't give A↔C).
cards.notes: Many VPCs → Transit Gateway.

cards.eli12: A private door from your network to AWS services.
cards.definition: Connect to AWS services over the private AWS network instead of the public internet. Gateway endpoints: S3 and DynamoDB. Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink): most other services.

cards.hint: AWS owned · AWS managed · Customer managed
cards.eli12: Who holds and controls the encryption keys.
cards.definition: AWS owned keys: used by AWS services for you, invisible and free. AWS managed keys (aws/service-name): in your account, managed and rotated by AWS. Customer managed keys: you create them and control policies and rotation; a monthly fee applies.

cards.hint: Scale · Disposable · Automate · Loose coupling · Services not servers
cards.eli12: AWS's rules of thumb for building good cloud apps.
cards.definition: AWS cloud best practices: design for scalability (vertical and horizontal); treat servers as disposable resources; automate (serverless, IaC, Auto Scaling); loose coupling so failures don't cascade (e.g., queues); use managed services instead of only EC2.

cards.hint: Business · People · Governance | Platform · Security · Operations
cards.eli12: The six viewpoints a company uses to plan its move to the cloud.
cards.definition: The six AWS CAF perspectives. Business capabilities: Business, People, Governance. Technical capabilities: Platform, Security, Operations.

cards.eli12: Four areas a company changes when it moves to the cloud.
cards.definition: The four CAF transformation domains: Technology (migrate and modernize), Process (digitize, automate, optimize operations), Organization (reorganize around products and value streams), Product (new value propositions and revenue models).

cards.eli12: Pushes new app versions onto your servers for you.
cards.definition: Automates application deployments to EC2 instances, on-premises servers, Lambda and ECS, with rolling or blue/green updates.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: AWS's version of GitHub.
cards.definition: Managed private Git repositories. AWS stopped onboarding new customers to CodeCommit in 2024.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A private shelf for the code libraries your apps use.
cards.definition: Managed artifact repository for storing and sharing software packages (e.g., npm, Maven, PyPI, NuGet).
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A database for readings over time, like sensor data.
cards.definition: Fully managed, serverless time-series database for data such as IoT sensor readings and application metrics.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A message post office that speaks the old standard languages.
cards.definition: Managed message broker for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. Used when migrating apps that rely on standard messaging protocols (MQTT, AMQP, STOMP) instead of rewriting them for SQS/SNS.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Helps you run a shared, tamper-proof ledger.
cards.definition: Fully managed service for creating and managing blockchain networks using open-source frameworks such as Hyperledger Fabric and Ethereum.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Suggests products people will probably like.
cards.definition: Fully managed machine learning service for building real-time personalized recommendations, based on the same technology used by Amazon.com.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A smart search engine for your company's files.
cards.definition: Machine learning-powered enterprise search that finds answers across documents and content repositories using natural-language questions.
cards.official: Amazon Kendra is an intelligent search service powered by ML.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Sends marketing texts and emails to the right customers.
cards.definition: Multichannel marketing communications service for sending targeted email, SMS, push notifications and voice messages to customers.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.hint: SATELLITE ground stations as a service
cards.eli12: Talk to satellites without building your own antenna.
cards.definition: Fully managed ground stations to control satellite communications and download and process satellite data, without building your own ground station infrastructure.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Try your app on lots of real phones in the cloud.
cards.definition: Tests web and mobile apps on real phones, tablets and desktop browsers hosted by AWS.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Lets apps get exactly the data they need from one API.
cards.definition: Managed service for building GraphQL and Pub/Sub APIs that let apps query and get real-time updates from multiple data sources.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A guard for the whole network, not just one server or website.
cards.definition: Managed network firewall that protects an entire VPC, with traffic filtering and intrusion prevention from Layer 3 to Layer 7.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: Draw your app's design and it writes the template for you.
cards.definition: Visual designer for building application architectures by dragging and connecting AWS resources. It generates infrastructure as code (CloudFormation templates). Formerly AWS Application Composer.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.hint: CHAOS testing: break things on purpose
cards.eli12: Practice failures on purpose to see if your app survives.
cards.definition: Managed service for running fault-injection (chaos engineering) experiments, such as stopping instances or adding latency, to test how resilient a workload is.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: AWS staff take care of your cloud for you.
cards.definition: AWS team that operates your AWS infrastructure for you, including monitoring, incident management, patching, backup and security.
cards.official: AWS Managed Services provides ongoing management of your AWS infrastructure so you can focus on your applications.
cards.notes: Not on the official CLF-C02 in-scope list. Mentioned in the course.

cards.eli12: A server is a computer with a brain (CPU), short-term memory (RAM), long-term storage and a network connection.
cards.definition: A server is made of compute (CPU), memory (RAM), storage (disk) and networking, and often runs a database to store data in a structured way.

cards.hint: ROUTER = between networks · SWITCH = inside a network
cards.eli12: A router is the post office between towns; a switch delivers mail to the right house on your street.
cards.definition: A router forwards data packets between different networks (it knows where to send traffic on the internet). A switch delivers packets to the right device inside a local network.

cards.hint: clients and servers find each other by IP ADDRESS
cards.eli12: Your browser (client) asks a server for a page using the server's address.
cards.definition: A client (like a web browser) sends requests over a network to a server, which sends responses back. Both have IP addresses; DNS turns website names into IP addresses.

cards.hint: RENT + POWER + slow HARDWARE + 24/7 STAFF + DISASTERS
cards.eli12: Running your own data center is expensive, slow and risky.
cards.definition: Running your own data center means paying rent, power, cooling and maintenance; waiting to add or replace hardware; limited scaling; a 24/7 team to monitor it; and exposure to disasters. The cloud takes these on for you.

cards.hint: ON-DEMAND IT over the internet, pay-as-you-go
cards.eli12: Renting computers, storage and apps over the internet instead of buying them.
cards.definition: On-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases, applications and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. You get exactly the type and size of resources you need, almost instantly, and AWS owns and maintains the hardware.
cards.official: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, database, storage, applications, and other IT resources through a cloud services platform via the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

cards.term: Private vs Public vs Hybrid Cloud
cards.hint: PRIVATE = yours alone · PUBLIC = provider's · HYBRID = both
cards.eli12: Private is your own kitchen, public is a restaurant, hybrid is cooking at home and ordering some dishes.
cards.definition: Private cloud: used by one organization, not exposed to the public, full control (good for sensitive apps). Public cloud: resources owned and run by a third-party provider like AWS and delivered over the internet. Hybrid cloud: keep some servers on-premises and extend into the cloud.

cards.hint: Flexible · Cost-effective · Scalable · Elastic · Highly available · Agile
cards.eli12: What the cloud fixes compared with running your own data center.
cards.definition: Flexibility (change resource types when needed), cost-effectiveness (pay for what you use), scalability (bigger or more machines), elasticity (scale out and in automatically), high availability and fault tolerance (build across data centers), and agility (build, test and launch fast).

cards.hint: pay for COMPUTE, STORAGE, DATA OUT (data IN is free)
cards.eli12: You pay for computer time, stored data and data leaving AWS.
cards.definition: AWS pay-as-you-go pricing is built on three things: compute time, data stored, and data transferred out of AWS. Data transferred in is free.

cards.hint: Pay as you go · Save when you reserve · Pay less by using more · Pay less as AWS grows
cards.eli12: Four ways AWS keeps prices low.
cards.definition: 1) Pay as you go: pay only for what you use. 2) Save when you reserve: commit for a discount (EC2 RIs, DynamoDB reserved capacity, ElastiCache reserved nodes, RDS RIs, Redshift reserved nodes). 3) Pay less by using more: volume discounts. 4) Pay less as AWS grows: prices drop over time.

cards.hint: GLOBAL: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, WAF · most others REGIONAL
cards.eli12: A few AWS services work everywhere at once; most live in the Region you pick.
cards.definition: A few services are global: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront and WAF. Most services are Region-scoped (e.g., EC2, Elastic Beanstalk, Lambda, Rekognition), so you choose a Region in the console. Not every service or feature is available in every Region.

cards.hint: no ROOT · 1 person = 1 user · GROUPS · MFA · ROLES · AUDIT
cards.eli12: The house rules for keeping AWS logins safe.
cards.definition: Don't use the root account except for account setup; one IAM user per person; assign permissions through groups; set a strong password policy; enforce MFA; use roles to give AWS services permissions; use access keys only for CLI/SDK; audit with the Credentials Report and Access Advisor; never share users or keys.

cards.eli12: Three doors into AWS: the website, the command line, and code.
cards.definition: Three ways to access AWS: the AWS Management Console (protected by password + MFA), the AWS CLI (access keys) and AWS SDKs inside your code (access keys). Access key ID ≈ username; secret access key ≈ password. Never share them.

cards.hint: a user gets permissions from EVERY group + inline policies
cards.eli12: You get the rules of every club you join, plus your own personal rules.
cards.definition: An IAM user receives the permissions of every group they belong to, plus any inline policy attached directly to them. Groups contain only users (not other groups); a user can be in several groups or none.

cards.hint: AWS = infrastructure · YOU = configuration, data, access
cards.eli12: Who does what, service by service.
cards.definition: IAM: you manage users, groups, roles, policies, MFA and key rotation. EC2: you patch the guest OS, set security groups and protect your data. EBS/EFS: you set up backups, snapshots and encryption; AWS replicates data and replaces hardware. S3: you set bucket policies, versioning and encryption; AWS guarantees durability and keeps customers separated. RDS: AWS patches the OS and database and disables SSH; you set security groups, database users, public access and encryption. Outposts: you handle the rack's physical security.

cards.eli12: An instance name tells you its family, version and size.
cards.definition: In a name like m5.2xlarge: m = instance class (family), 5 = generation, 2xlarge = size within the class. Families: general purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, storage optimized, accelerated computing, HPC optimized.

cards.eli12: Super-powered servers for giant science problems.
cards.definition: Instances built for high-performance computing at scale, such as large, complex simulations and deep learning workloads.

cards.hint: SSH = remote command line on PORT 22
cards.eli12: Typing commands on a faraway Linux computer as if you were sitting at it.
cards.definition: Protocol for securely controlling a remote Linux machine from the command line over port 22, using a key pair. Windows users can use PuTTY. Alternatives without managing keys: EC2 Instance Connect and Systems Manager Session Manager.

cards.hint: TIMEOUT = security group · CONNECTION REFUSED = the app
cards.eli12: How to tell a firewall problem from an app problem.
cards.definition: Security groups can be attached to many instances, are tied to one Region/VPC and sit outside the instance (blocked traffic never reaches it). A timeout usually means a security group is blocking; 'connection refused' means the app isn't running or errored. Rules can reference IP ranges or other security groups. Keep a separate group for SSH.

cards.hint: CONVERTIBLE = can change family/OS · smaller discount
cards.eli12: A reservation you can swap later, in exchange for a slightly smaller discount.
cards.definition: Reserved Instances you can exchange to change the instance family, type, OS, scope or tenancy. The discount is smaller than Standard RIs (up to about 66% vs 72%), and they can't be sold on the RI Marketplace.

cards.hint: On-Demand = walk-in · RI = book ahead · Savings Plan = $/hr any room · Spot = bid, may be kicked out · Dedicated Host = whole building · Capacity Reservation = pay for the room even if empty
cards.eli12: Picture EC2 pricing as booking a hotel.
cards.definition: On-Demand: arrive any time, pay full price. Reserved: plan a long stay for a discount. Savings Plans: pay a set amount per hour and stay in any room type. Spot: bid for empty rooms and can be kicked out at any time. Dedicated Host: book the whole building. Capacity Reservation: book a room at full price whether you use it or not.

cards.hint: ROOT volume deleted by default · extra volumes kept
cards.eli12: Whether a drive is thrown away when its server is deleted.
cards.definition: Attribute controlling whether an EBS volume is deleted when its instance terminates. Enabled by default for the root volume, disabled by default for other attached volumes. Turn it off on the root volume to keep the data.

cards.hint: AUTOMATE building, testing and sharing AMIs
cards.eli12: A robot that builds and tests your server templates for you.
cards.definition: Free service (you pay only for underlying resources) that automates creating, maintaining, testing and distributing AMIs or container images, on a schedule if you like, and can share them across Regions.

cards.hint: EBS = ONE instance, ONE AZ · EFS = MANY instances, MANY AZs
cards.eli12: EBS is a USB stick for one computer; EFS is a shared network drive for the whole office.
cards.definition: EBS: block storage attached to one instance in one AZ (move it to another AZ with a snapshot); you pay for provisioned size. EFS: shared NFS file system that hundreds of Linux instances across AZs can mount at once; pay per use, higher price per GB.

cards.term: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
cards.eli12: A shared Windows network drive, run by AWS.
cards.definition: Fully managed, native Windows shared file system built on Windows File Server: supports SMB and NTFS, integrates with Microsoft Active Directory, and can be reached from AWS or on-premises.

cards.eli12: A super-fast file system for supercomputer-style jobs.
cards.definition: Fully managed, high-performance file system for HPC, machine learning, analytics, video processing and financial modeling. Can link to S3; scales to hundreds of GB/s, millions of IOPS and sub-millisecond latency.
confuse: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

cards.hint: SCALE = handle MORE load · HA = SURVIVE a data-center loss
cards.eli12: Scaling is hiring more call-center operators; high availability is having a second office in another city.
cards.definition: Scalability means a system can handle greater load by adapting: vertically (bigger instance) or horizontally (more instances). High availability means running in at least 2 Availability Zones so the app survives losing a data center. They're linked (HA usually goes with horizontal scaling) but different.

cards.hint: Scalable = CAN grow · Elastic = grows AUTOMATICALLY · Agility = SPEED (distractor)
cards.eli12: Three words that sound alike but mean different things.
cards.definition: Scalability: able to handle more load by scaling up or out. Elasticity: once scalable, it scales automatically with the load (pay per use, match demand). Agility: not about scaling — new IT resources are a click away, so teams get them in minutes instead of weeks.

cards.hint: spread traffic · health checks · one DNS name · HTTPS
cards.eli12: A traffic cop sending visitors to whichever server is free and healthy.
cards.definition: A load balancer forwards incoming traffic to multiple servers. Benefits: spreads load, gives one point of access (DNS name), handles failed instances through health checks, provides SSL/HTTPS termination and high availability across AZs. ELB is AWS-managed, so AWS handles upgrades, maintenance and availability.

cards.hint: ASG = fleet with MIN / DESIRED / MAX
cards.eli12: A team of servers that grows when it's busy and shrinks when it's quiet.
cards.definition: A group of EC2 instances that scales out when load rises and in when it falls, keeps the count between a minimum and maximum, replaces unhealthy instances and automatically registers new instances with a load balancer. Saves money by running only what's needed.

cards.hint: BUCKET = top-level container, created in a REGION
cards.eli12: A bucket is a big labeled box you put files in.
cards.definition: Containers for S3 objects. Buckets are created in a specific Region, even though S3 looks global. Names must be globally unique (or unique within your account and Region if you use the newer account regional namespace): lowercase, no underscores, not an IP address, starting with a letter or number.

cards.hint: OBJECT = KEY (full path) + data (up to 50 TB)
cards.eli12: A file in S3, with its full name and some sticky notes about it.
cards.definition: Files stored in S3. Each has a key (the full path: prefix + name; there are no real folders, just names with slashes), the data itself (up to 50 TB; use multipart upload above 5 GB), metadata, up to 10 tags and a version ID if versioning is on.

cards.term: S3 Security (IAM vs Bucket Policy vs ACL)
cards.hint: IAM policy = USER-based · Bucket policy/ACL = RESOURCE-based
cards.eli12: Two ways to say who can open a bucket: rules on the person, or rules on the bucket.
cards.definition: User-based: IAM policies control which S3 API calls a user can make. Resource-based: bucket policies (bucket-wide rules; allow public or cross-account access), plus object and bucket ACLs (finer-grained, can be disabled). Access is allowed if the IAM policy OR the resource policy allows it AND nothing explicitly denies it. Give EC2 access with IAM roles.
confuse: S3 Bucket Policies & Block Public Access

cards.hint: S3 can host STATIC websites (403 = allow public reads)
cards.eli12: S3 can be the home of a simple website.
cards.definition: S3 can serve a static website from a bucket, at a website URL that includes the Region. A 403 Forbidden error usually means the bucket policy doesn't allow public reads.

cards.hint: 11 9s DURABILITY for every class · AVAILABILITY varies by class
cards.eli12: Durable = your file won't be lost; available = you can get it right now.
cards.definition: Durability (99.999999999%, the same for every storage class) is about not losing objects: storing 10 million objects, expect to lose one about every 10,000 years. Availability is how often data is reachable and varies by class: Standard 99.99% (about 53 minutes down a year), Standard-IA 99.9%, One Zone-IA 99.5%.

cards.hint: TABLES linked together, queried with SQL
cards.eli12: Like spreadsheets with links between them.
cards.definition: Store data in tables with defined relationships, queried with SQL; used for transactional apps (OLTP). On AWS: Amazon RDS and Aurora.

cards.eli12: Databases that don't need a fixed table layout.
cards.definition: Non-relational databases built for specific data models with flexible schemas: easy to evolve, scale out across clusters, high performance. Types: key-value, document (JSON), graph, in-memory, search. On AWS: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Neptune, ElastiCache, OpenSearch.

cards.eli12: OLTP is the cash register; OLAP is the end-of-year sales report.
cards.definition: OLTP (online transaction processing): many small reads and writes from apps — RDS, Aurora. OLAP (online analytical processing): large analytic queries over big data loaded in batches — Redshift (columnar data warehouse).

cards.hint: Aurora that SCALES ITSELF, pay per second
cards.eli12: A database that turns itself up and down as needed.
cards.definition: Aurora option that automatically starts and scales database capacity with actual usage: no capacity planning, pay per second. Good for infrequent, intermittent or unpredictable workloads. Supports MySQL and PostgreSQL.

cards.hint: read replicas in OTHER Regions = DR + fast local reads
cards.eli12: Copies of your database in other countries for faraway readers and for emergencies.
cards.definition: Read replicas placed in other Regions give disaster recovery if a Region fails and low-latency reads for users around the world. Writes still go to the main database; cross-Region replication costs apply.

cards.hint: DynamoDB in many Regions — read AND write anywhere
cards.eli12: The same table kept in sync around the world.
cards.definition: Replicates a DynamoDB table across multiple Regions with active-active (two-way) replication, so users can read and write with low latency in any of them.

cards.eli12: Run big reports without setting up the warehouse yourself.
cards.definition: Runs Redshift analytics without managing data warehouse infrastructure: capacity is provisioned and scaled automatically and you pay only for what you use. Good for reporting, dashboards and real-time analytics.

cards.hint: CATALOG of your datasets for Athena, Redshift, EMR
cards.eli12: A library card catalog for your data.
cards.definition: Central catalog of metadata about your datasets (schemas, locations) that Athena, Redshift and EMR use to find and query data.

cards.hint: VMs each have a GUEST OS · containers SHARE the host OS
cards.eli12: VMs are separate houses; containers are apartments in one building.
cards.definition: VMs each run a full guest OS on a hypervisor. Containers share the host's OS through the Docker daemon, so many more fit on one server and they start in seconds. Images are stored in Docker Hub (public) or Amazon ECR (private).

cards.eli12: A manager that decides where all your containers run.
cards.definition: Open-source, cloud-agnostic system for deploying, managing and scaling containerized apps. AWS runs it for you as Amazon EKS, on EC2 instances or Fargate.

cards.hint: pay per REQUEST + per GB-SECOND (generous free tier)
cards.eli12: You pay for how many times your code runs and how long it runs.
cards.definition: Billed per request ($0.20 per million after the first 1 million free each month) and per duration × memory in GB-seconds (400,000 GB-seconds free each month). Functions can have up to 10 GB of memory; more memory also gives more CPU and network.

cards.hint: LAMBDA = short serverless (15 min) · BATCH = long jobs in Docker on EC2
cards.eli12: Lambda is a quick errand; Batch is a long shift.
cards.definition: Lambda: 15-minute limit, limited runtimes and temporary disk, serverless. Batch: no time limit, any runtime packaged as a Docker image, uses EBS/instance store for disk, runs on EC2 or Spot instances managed by AWS.

cards.eli12: A recipe that builds your cloud setup the same way every time.
cards.definition: Managing infrastructure through templates or code instead of manual clicks: repeatable, reviewable, version-controlled, and easy to delete and recreate (e.g., turn off dev at night). On AWS: CloudFormation (declarative JSON/YAML templates) and CDK (programming languages).

cards.hint: ELB → EC2 in an ASG (multi-AZ) → RDS + ElastiCache
cards.eli12: The classic web app: front door, workers, and a database with a fast cache.
cards.definition: Common design for web apps: a load balancer in front of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across AZs, with RDS for data and ElastiCache for session data and caching.

cards.hint: Single instance (dev) · LB + ASG (prod web) · ASG only (workers)
cards.eli12: Three ready-made layouts Beanstalk can build for you.
cards.definition: Beanstalk architectures: single instance (good for dev), load balancer + Auto Scaling group (production web apps), Auto Scaling group only (non-web workers). A health agent pushes metrics to CloudWatch. Beanstalk handles the OS, capacity, load balancing and scaling; only your code is your responsibility.

cards.eli12: An assembly line that tests and ships code changes for you.
cards.definition: Continuous integration and continuous delivery: automatically build, test and release every code change. On AWS: CodeCommit (source), CodeBuild (build and test), CodeDeploy (deploy), CodePipeline (orchestrates the whole pipeline).

cards.hint: secure shell WITHOUT SSH, keys or port 22
cards.eli12: Log in to a server through AWS without opening any doors.
cards.definition: Starts a secure shell on EC2 or on-premises servers through the SSM agent, with no SSH keys, bastion hosts or open port 22. Access is controlled with IAM, and session logs can be sent to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.

cards.hint: store CONFIG and secrets (no automatic rotation)
cards.eli12: A safe drawer for settings and passwords.
cards.definition: Secure, serverless storage for configuration values and secrets (plain text or encrypted with KMS), with version tracking and IAM access control. Unlike Secrets Manager, it doesn't rotate secrets automatically.

cards.hint: LOW LATENCY + DISASTER RECOVERY + harder to ATTACK
cards.eli12: Putting your app in many places around the world.
cards.definition: Apps deployed in multiple Regions and/or edge locations: lower latency for users everywhere, failover to another Region in a disaster, and a spread-out footprint that's harder to attack. Tools: Route 53, CloudFront, S3 Transfer Acceleration, Global Accelerator.

cards.hint: LATENCY = how long data takes to travel
cards.eli12: The delay between asking for something and getting it.
cards.definition: The time it takes a network packet to travel between a user and a server. Reduced by deploying closer to users (Regions, Local Zones, edge locations, Wavelength).

cards.hint: A = IPv4 · AAAA = IPv6 · CNAME = name→name · Alias = name→AWS resource
cards.eli12: Different kinds of address-book entries.
cards.definition: A record: hostname → IPv4. AAAA: hostname → IPv6. CNAME: hostname → another hostname. Alias: hostname → an AWS resource such as an ELB, CloudFront distribution, S3 website or RDS.

cards.eli12: Different rules for which server a visitor is sent to.
cards.definition: Simple: one resource, no health checks. Weighted: split traffic by percentage (e.g., 70/20/10). Latency: send users to the Region with the lowest latency. Failover: send traffic to a standby when the primary fails its health check (disaster recovery).

cards.hint: ORIGIN = where CloudFront gets the content (S3, ALB, EC2, HTTP)
cards.eli12: The warehouse CloudFront restocks its local shops from.
cards.definition: CloudFront fetches content from an origin and caches it at edge locations. Origins: an S3 bucket (secured with Origin Access Control + bucket policy), a VPC origin (private ALB, NLB or EC2), or any custom HTTP backend such as a public ALB or S3 website.

cards.hint: CloudFront = CACHE everywhere (static) · CRR = live copies in a FEW Regions (dynamic)
cards.eli12: Cached copies worldwide vs a live twin in another Region.
cards.definition: CloudFront caches files across the global edge network for a time-to-live (TTL); best for static content needed everywhere. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies objects in near real time to specific Regions you set up; read-only, best for dynamic content needed with low latency in a few Regions.

cards.hint: CloudFront CACHES content · Global Accelerator PROXIES traffic (TCP/UDP, static IPs)
cards.eli12: One stores copies near you; the other gives you a faster road to the original.
cards.definition: Both use the AWS global network and edge locations and integrate with Shield. CloudFront is a CDN that caches content like images and video at the edge. Global Accelerator doesn't cache: it proxies packets to apps in AWS Regions, works for TCP/UDP, gives static IP addresses and fast regional failover.

cards.hint: ACTIVE-PASSIVE = standby Region · ACTIVE-ACTIVE = all Regions serve
cards.eli12: One store open with a backup store closed vs every store open.
cards.definition: Global designs from simple to complex: single Region single AZ; single Region multi-AZ (high availability); multi-Region active-passive (one Region serves traffic, another waits for failover); multi-Region active-active (every Region serves reads and writes — lowest latency, most complex).

cards.hint: decouple with a QUEUE (SQS), PUB/SUB (SNS) or STREAM (Kinesis)
cards.eli12: Instead of calling each other directly, apps leave messages in a shared mailbox.
cards.definition: Direct (synchronous) app-to-app calls can break during traffic spikes. Asynchronous, event-based communication through a middle service decouples apps so each part scales on its own: SQS (queue), SNS (pub/sub), Kinesis (real-time streaming).

cards.eli12: First in line, first served.
cards.definition: SQS queue type that keeps messages in the exact order they were sent (first in, first out). Standard queues offer maximum throughput but don't guarantee order.

cards.hint: FIREHOSE = load streaming data INTO S3 / Redshift / OpenSearch
cards.eli12: A pipe that pours a stream of data into storage.
cards.definition: Fully managed service that delivers streaming data (for example from Kinesis Data Streams) into destinations such as S3, Redshift and OpenSearch.

cards.hint: METRIC = variable you monitor (CPU, not RAM by default)
cards.eli12: Numbers AWS tracks about your stuff over time.
cards.definition: Time-stamped values for every AWS service, viewable in dashboards. EC2 sends CPU, status checks and network every 5 minutes by default (every 1 minute with paid detailed monitoring), but not RAM. Other examples: S3 bucket size, billing estimated charges (us-east-1 only), custom metrics.

cards.hint: ALARM on a metric → Auto Scaling, EC2 action or SNS
cards.eli12: An alarm clock that goes off when a number gets too high or low.
cards.definition: Trigger notifications or actions when a metric crosses a threshold: adjust Auto Scaling capacity, stop/terminate/reboot/recover an EC2 instance, or notify an SNS topic. States: OK, INSUFFICIENT_DATA, ALARM.

cards.hint: AUTOMATIC detection of unusual API activity
cards.eli12: CloudTrail noticing when something weird is going on.
cards.definition: CloudTrail feature that automatically analyzes events to detect unusual API activity. Reminders: CloudTrail is on by default, a trail can cover all Regions, logs can go to CloudWatch Logs or S3, and it's the first place to check when a resource was deleted.

cards.hint: Public IPv4 changes on stop/start · Private stays · Elastic IP = fixed · IPv6 free
cards.eli12: Different kinds of addresses for your servers.
cards.definition: Public IPv4: reachable on the internet; an EC2 instance gets a new one each time it stops and starts; all public IPv4 addresses (including Elastic IPs) are billed hourly. Private IPv4: for internal networks; stays the same. Elastic IP: a fixed public IPv4. IPv6: every address is public, and it's free.

cards.hint: Site-to-Site VPN = CUSTOMER GATEWAY (on-prem) + VIRTUAL PRIVATE GATEWAY (AWS)
cards.eli12: The two ends of the tunnel.
cards.definition: A Site-to-Site VPN needs a Customer Gateway on the on-premises side and a Virtual Private Gateway on the AWS (VPC) side.

cards.hint: DDoS = flood of traffic from MANY bots
cards.eli12: A crowd of fake visitors jamming the door so real customers can't get in.
cards.definition: Distributed denial-of-service: attackers use many machines (bots) to flood an application or server so legitimate users can't reach it.

cards.eli12: The layers AWS uses to stop traffic floods.
cards.definition: Shield Standard (free, automatic), Shield Advanced (24/7 response team, cost protection), WAF (filter requests, rate-based rules), CloudFront and Route 53 (absorb attacks across the global edge network), and Auto Scaling to handle extra load.

cards.hint: OPT-IN: EBS, S3 SSE-KMS, RDS, Redshift, EFS · AUTOMATIC: CloudTrail logs, S3 Glacier, Storage Gateway
cards.eli12: Some services lock your data only if you ask; others always do.
cards.definition: If a question mentions encryption on AWS, think KMS. You opt in to encryption for EBS volumes, S3 with SSE-KMS (SSE-S3 is on by default), RDS, Redshift and EFS. Encryption is automatic for CloudTrail logs, S3 Glacier and Storage Gateway.

cards.hint: only ROOT can: change account settings, CLOSE account, change SUPPORT PLAN, sell RIs…
cards.eli12: The jobs only the account owner can do.
cards.definition: Tasks only the root user can do: change account settings (name, email, root password and keys); view certain tax invoices; close the account; restore IAM user permissions; change or cancel the support plan; register as a seller in the RI Marketplace; enable MFA Delete on an S3 bucket; edit or delete a broken S3 bucket policy; sign up for GovCloud.

cards.term: If Your AWS Account Is Compromised
cards.hint: change ROOT password · rotate ALL keys/passwords · contact AWS Support
cards.eli12: What to do right away if someone breaks in.
cards.definition: Change the root password, delete and rotate all passwords and access keys, and contact AWS Support.

cards.hint: OU = folder of accounts (by team, environment or project)
cards.eli12: Folders that group your AWS accounts.
cards.definition: Groups of accounts inside AWS Organizations, nested under the root, organized by business unit, environment (dev/prod) or project. SCPs can be attached to OUs to limit what their accounts can do.

cards.hint: separate ACCOUNTS for teams, environments, compliance and logging
cards.eli12: Giving each team or environment its own AWS account.
cards.definition: Create accounts per department, cost center or environment (dev/test/prod) for isolation, separate service quotas and compliance (with SCPs). Use tagging standards for billing, and send CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs from every account to a central logging account.

cards.hint: new accounts: up to $200 CREDITS · Free Plan (6 months) or Paid Plan
cards.eli12: How new AWS accounts get free money to learn with.
cards.definition: New accounts get up to $200 in credits and choose a Free Plan (ends after 6 months or when credits run out, with no charges) or a Paid Plan (charged once credits are used). Both include Always Free offers such as Lambda's 1 million requests and DynamoDB's 25 GB each month.

cards.hint: instances × (type, size, Region, OS) + purchase option + ELB + detailed monitoring
cards.eli12: What makes an EC2 bill bigger or smaller.
cards.definition: EC2 cost depends on the number of instances, instance type and size, Region, OS and software, and purchasing option, plus extras such as load balancer hours and data processed and detailed monitoring. On-Demand bills per second for Linux/Windows (60-second minimum) or per hour for other OSes.

cards.hint: ECS on EC2 = pay for the EC2 · Fargate = pay for vCPU + memory
cards.eli12: Either rent the servers, or pay just for what the containers use.
cards.definition: ECS with the EC2 launch type has no extra fee: you pay for the EC2 instances and other resources you create. Fargate launch type: you pay for the vCPU and memory allocated to your containers.

cards.term: Service Pricing Factors (S3, EBS, RDS, CloudFront)
cards.hint: S3: class + size + requests + data out · EBS: provisioned GB + IOPS + snapshots · RDS: hours + engine + size + storage · CloudFront: data out + requests
cards.eli12: What drives the bill for common services.
cards.definition: S3: storage class, amount stored, number and type of requests, data out of the Region, Transfer Acceleration, lifecycle transitions. EBS: volume type, provisioned GB per month, provisioned IOPS, snapshots. RDS: per-hour billing by engine, size and memory class, purchase type, extra storage, I/O, Single- or Multi-AZ (backup storage free up to 100% of database storage). CloudFront: data out and HTTP/HTTPS requests, priced by geography. Inbound data is free.

cards.hint: ESTIMATE: Pricing Calculator · TRACK: Billing Dashboard, tags, CUR, Cost Explorer · MONITOR: billing alarms, Budgets
cards.eli12: Which money tool to use when.
cards.definition: Estimating costs: AWS Pricing Calculator. Tracking costs: Billing Dashboard, cost allocation tags, Cost and Usage Reports, Cost Explorer. Monitoring against plans: CloudWatch billing alarms and AWS Budgets. Also: Savings Plans, Cost Anomaly Detection, Compute Optimizer, Service Quotas.

cards.eli12: The summary page of your AWS bill.
cards.definition: Billing console page with a high-level view of month-to-date and forecasted charges and spend by service.

cards.hint: AD = Windows' central database of users and computers
cards.eli12: The company phone book that also decides who can log in where.
cards.definition: Directory service on Windows Server (AD Domain Services) that stores users, computers, printers, file shares and security groups for centralized login and permissions.

cards.hint: Managed AD (full AD in AWS) · AD Connector (proxy to on-prem) · Simple AD (basic, standalone)
cards.eli12: Three ways to use Active Directory with AWS.
cards.definition: AWS Managed Microsoft AD: real AD in AWS, manage users there, supports MFA and trust with on-prem AD. AD Connector: proxy that sends logins to your on-premises AD (users stay on-prem). Simple AD: basic AD-compatible directory on AWS that can't join on-prem AD.

cards.hint: DaaS = desktops delivered from the CLOUD
cards.eli12: Your work computer runs in AWS and you just log in.
cards.definition: Virtual desktops hosted in the cloud instead of on-premises VDI (virtual desktop infrastructure). Amazon WorkSpaces gives users full Windows/Linux desktops; AppStream 2.0 streams individual applications to a browser.

cards.eli12: Pick up the whole house and put it down in the cloud unchanged.
cards.definition: Migrate applications, databases or servers to AWS without changes or cloud optimizations. Simple and fast; can still save around 30%. Example tool: AWS Application Migration Service.

cards.hint: REPLATFORM = small cloud tweaks, same architecture
cards.eli12: Move the house and swap in a few better appliances.
cards.definition: Keep the core architecture but use some cloud optimizations, such as moving a database to RDS or an app to Elastic Beanstalk, to save time and money with managed or serverless services.

cards.eli12: Tear down and rebuild the house for the new neighborhood.
cards.definition: Reimagine the application using cloud-native features, driven by needs for new features, scale, performance, security or agility — for example, moving from a monolith to microservices or serverless.

cards.hint: REPURCHASE = switch to a different product (often SaaS)
cards.eli12: Throw out the old appliance and buy a new brand.
cards.definition: Move to a different product while migrating, often SaaS (e.g., CRM to Salesforce, HR to Workday). More expensive short-term but quick to deploy.

cards.eli12: Throw away what you don't use before moving.
cards.definition: Turn off applications you no longer need. Saves cost, shrinks the attack surface and lets teams focus on what matters.

cards.hint: RETAIN = keep it where it is FOR NOW
cards.eli12: Leave it in the old house for now.
cards.definition: Decide not to migrate yet, for reasons like security, compliance, performance, unresolved dependencies or no business value (e.g., mainframes).

cards.hint: RELOCATE = move to the cloud VERSION of the same platform
cards.eli12: Move to the same kind of building in a new city.
cards.definition: Move apps to the cloud version of their platform without changing them (e.g., VMware to VMware Cloud on AWS), or move EC2 instances to a different VPC, account or Region.

cards.hint: Stop guessing capacity · Test at production scale · Automate · Evolve · Data-driven · Game days
cards.eli12: AWS's general rules for good cloud design.
cards.definition: Stop guessing capacity needs; test systems at production scale; automate to make experimenting easier; allow architectures to evolve with changing requirements; drive architecture decisions with data; improve through game days (simulate events like flash-sale traffic).

cards.hint: run, monitor, IMPROVE: operations as code, small reversible changes
cards.eli12: Running things smoothly and getting better every time.
cards.definition: Run and monitor systems to deliver business value and keep improving processes. Principles: operations as code, frequent small reversible changes, refine procedures often, anticipate failure, learn from failures, use managed services, observability. Services: CloudFormation, Config, CloudTrail, CloudWatch, X-Ray, CodeBuild, CodePipeline.
